studyPages.title: Matter and Pure Substances
studyPages.body:
MATTER AND PURE SUBSTANCES
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what matter and pure substances means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show matter and pure substances.
• Correct one common mistake about matter and pure substances.

INTRODUCTION
----
Hold a stone, a cup of milk and the air you breathe — all three are matter because each occupies space and has mass. Scientists then ask a sharper question: is the sample a pure substance with one fixed composition, or a mixture of different materials? Pure substances are either elements or compounds; mixtures can be uniform like salt water or non-uniform like sandy soil.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass.
• Matter is composed of pure substances and mixtures.
• The pure substances can be element and compounds while the mixtures can either be uniform or non-uniform.
• An element is a pure substance which cannot be made simpler using chemical means.
• Elements are the building blocks of matter. Everything around is made up of an element or elements.
• A compound is a pure substance that consists of atoms of two or more elements that are chemically joined together.
• Pure substances either elements or compounds has a unique name and symbol.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked situation (a hardware shop in Nakuru): a learner investigates matter and pure substances. First observation: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a hardware shop in Nakuru, matter and pure substances shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Safety tip: if you see smoke, raise the alarm early and do not fight a large fire alone.

SUMMARY
----
• Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass.
• Matter is composed of pure substances and mixtures.
• The pure substances can be element and compounds while the mixtures can either be uniform or non-uniform.
• An element is a pure substance which cannot be made simpler using chemical means.

REVISION QUESTIONS
----
1. Define matter and pure substances in your own words and give one clear example.
2. Describe a situation at a hardware shop in Nakuru that shows matter and pure substances, and explain the science involved.
3. A learner makes a mistake about matter and pure substances. State a likely wrong idea, correct it, and justify your correction with facts from this page.

ANSWERS
----
1. The pure substances can be element and compounds while the mixtures can either be uniform or non-uniform. For example, link it to a real object or event at home, school, market or shamba that fits this page.
2. At a hardware shop in Nakuru, you would observe something that matches matter and pure substances. Name the observation, then explain it using the definition above. End by stating why the correct idea matters for accuracy or safety.
3. Wrong idea: confusing matter and pure substances with a neighbouring concept or ignoring a key rule. Correct idea: Define matter; pure substances vs mixtures. Justification: the worked example on this page shows the right reasoning with real objects or numbers.

studyPages.title: What Is an Element
studyPages.body:
WHAT IS AN ELEMENT
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• What makes a substance an element.
• How to tell an element apart from a compound.
• Some common elements you meet every day and their symbols.

INTRODUCTION
----
Look at a copper electrical wire, a gold earring, and the oxygen you are breathing right now. Each one is made of a single, pure building block that scientists call an element. Everything around you is built from just over 100 of these building blocks.

MAIN NOTES
----
• An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into a simpler substance by any chemical or physical means.
• An element is made of only ONE kind of atom. For example, a piece of pure copper contains only copper atoms.
• There are about 118 known elements. Each one has its own name and its own short symbol, for example oxygen (O), hydrogen (H), carbon (C), iron (Fe), copper (Cu) and gold (Au).
• A symbol is usually the first letter of the name written as a capital, sometimes with a second small letter. Some come from Latin: iron is Fe from "ferrum", gold is Au from "aurum".
• Elements are the building blocks of matter. They can exist on their own, or join with other elements to form compounds. Table salt, NaCl, is not an element — it is a compound made from the elements sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl).

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
A learner in Nakuru buys a jembe. The blade is made mainly of iron. Is iron an element? Iron cannot be split into anything simpler than iron atoms, so YES — iron (Fe) is an element. Now the same learner points at the rust forming on an old blade left in the rain. Is rust an element? No. Rust forms when iron joins with oxygen from the air. Because it now contains two different elements joined together, rust is a compound, not an element.

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
The aluminium (Al) in a cooking sufuria and the copper (Cu) in phone-charger wires are both elements you handle at home near a kitchen in Kisumu. Safety tip: never heat an unknown metal or chemical in the kitchen to "test" it — some give off harmful fumes; only do heating tests under a teacher's guidance in the lab.

SUMMARY
----
• An element cannot be broken into anything simpler.
• It is made of only one kind of atom.
• Each element has a name and a symbol (O, Fe, Cu, Au).
• Two or more elements join to make compounds like NaCl and rust.

REVISION QUESTIONS
----
1. Define an element and give two examples found in a Kenyan home.
2. A student says, "Salt (NaCl) is an element because it looks pure and white." Explain why this is wrong.
3. A jembe left in the rain forms rust. Explain why rust cannot be called an element.

ANSWERS
----
1. An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into a simpler substance by chemical or physical means, because it is made of only one kind of atom. Two examples in a Kenyan home are the copper (Cu) in electrical wires and the aluminium (Al) in a cooking sufuria.
2. Salt is not an element; it is a compound. Even though it looks pure and white, sodium chloride is made of two different elements — sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl) — chemically joined. Because it contains more than one kind of atom and can be split into sodium and chlorine, it is a compound.
3. Rust cannot be called an element because it is a compound called iron oxide. It forms when iron (Fe) reacts with oxygen (O) from the air and water. Since it is made of two elements joined chemically, it is no longer a single pure building block.

studyPages.title: Atoms as Building Units
studyPages.body:
ATOMS AS BUILDING UNITS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what atoms as building units means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show atoms as building units.
• Correct one common mistake about atoms as building units.

INTRODUCTION
----
If you could zoom into a pure copper wire until you reached the smallest piece that is still copper, you would be looking at a copper atom. An atom is the smallest particle of an element that still represents that element. Atoms of the same element are chemically identical, which is why every pure copper sample behaves like copper.

MAIN NOTES
----
• An element is made of atoms.
• Atoms of the same element are identical.
• Compounds are formed when atoms of different elements react.
• An element is a substance that cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical or physical means.
• Compounds can be broken down into elements through chemical reactions.
• Sodium and chlorine are elements that combine chemically to form sodium chloride which is a compound.
• Relating common elements to their symbols.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked situation (Lake Magadi salt works): a learner investigates atoms as building units. First observation: An element is made of atoms. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At Lake Magadi salt works, atoms as building units shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Practical tip: compare two cases (right vs wrong) so the idea sticks for exams.

SUMMARY
----
• An element is made of atoms.
• Atoms of the same element are identical.
• Compounds are formed when atoms of different elements react.
• An element is a substance that cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical or physical means.

studyPages.title: What Is a Compound
studyPages.body:
WHAT IS A COMPOUND
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what what is a compound means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show what is a compound.
• Correct one common mistake about what is a compound.

INTRODUCTION
----
Sodium metal reacts violently with water, and chlorine gas is poisonous — yet together they form ordinary table salt you eat. That is the power of a compound: different elements join chemically in fixed proportions and create a new substance with new properties. Water (H₂O) and salt (NaCl) are everyday compounds built this way.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A compound is a pure substance formed when atoms of two or more different elements join chemically in fixed proportions.
• Water is a compound with formula H₂O: two hydrogen atoms join one oxygen atom.
• Common salt is a compound with formula NaCl: sodium and chlorine join in a 1:1 ratio.
• Compounds can only be broken into their elements by chemical methods, not by simple physical sorting.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked situation (Marikiti market in Nairobi): a learner investigates what is a compound. First observation: Compounds are represented by a chemical formula. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At Marikiti market in Nairobi, what is a compound shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Safety tip: if you see smoke, raise the alarm early and do not fight a large fire alone.

SUMMARY
----
• A compound is a pure substance formed when atoms of two or more different elements join chemically in fixed proportions.
• Water is a compound with formula H₂O: two hydrogen atoms join one oxygen atom.
• Common salt is a compound with formula NaCl: sodium and chlorine join in a 1:1 ratio.
• Compounds can only be broken into their elements by chemical methods, not by simple physical sorting.

REVISION QUESTIONS
----

2. Describe a situation at Marikiti market in Nairobi that shows what is a compound, and explain the science involved.
3. A learner makes a mistake about what is a compound. State a likely wrong idea, correct it, and justify your correction with facts from this page.

ANSWERS
----
1. A compound is a pure substance formed when atoms of two or more different elements join chemically in fixed proportions. For example, link it to a real object or event at home, school, market or shamba that fits this page.
2. At Marikiti market in Nairobi, you would observe something that matches what is a compound. Name the observation, then explain it using the definition above, including the correct formula or symbol. End by stating why the correct idea matters for accuracy or safety.
3. Wrong idea: confusing what is a compound with a neighbouring concept or ignoring a key rule. Correct idea: Compound formation and fixed proportions. Justification: the worked example on this page shows the right reasoning with real objects or numbers.

studyPages.title: Elements Versus Compounds
studyPages.body:
ELEMENTS VERSUS COMPOUNDS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what elements versus compounds means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show elements versus compounds.
• Correct one common mistake about elements versus compounds.

INTRODUCTION
----
A pure iron nail and a pile of table salt can both look "simple," but only one is an element. The nail is made of iron atoms alone. Salt is made of sodium and chlorine joined chemically. The quick test is: can you break it into different elements by chemical means? If yes, it is a compound; if it is already a single kind of atom, it is an element.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A chemical symbol is usually derived from first letter of the English name of the element. It is also derived from Latin name of the element.
• Some elements might start with same first letters, such as Carbon, Calcium, Chlorine and Copper have their names starting with letter C, therefore letter C can not be used to represent all of them as chemical symbol.

studyPages.title: Rules for Writing Chemical Symbols
studyPages.body:
RULES FOR WRITING CHEMICAL SYMBOLS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what rules for writing chemical symbols means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show rules for writing chemical symbols.
• Correct one common mistake about rules for writing chemical symbols.

INTRODUCTION
----
Write Co and you mean the metal cobalt. Write CO and you mean carbon monoxide, a dangerous compound. One capital letter changed the meaning completely. Chemical symbols follow a strict capitalization rule so that every scientist, in every language, reads the same substance.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A chemical symbol is a short universal code for an element's name so scientists everywhere understand each other.
• The first letter of a symbol is ALWAYS a capital letter. If there is a second letter, it MUST be a small letter.
• Example: calcium is Ca, not CA or ca. Copper is Cu. Cobalt is Co — but CO (both capitals) means the compound carbon monoxide, not cobalt.
• Some symbols come from English names (H, O, C). Others come from Latin names (Na from Natrium for sodium, Fe from Ferrum for iron).

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
At a school lab in Machakos, a learner labels a cobalt sample as CO on a chart. The teacher crosses it out. CO (both capitals) stands for carbon monoxide, a compound of carbon and oxygen. Cobalt the element must be written Co — capital C, small o. The same learner then writes calcium as CA. That is also wrong; calcium is Ca. Rule used: first letter capital, second letter small.

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a school lab in Machakos, rules for writing chemical symbols shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Safety tip: if you see smoke, raise the alarm early and do not fight a large fire alone.

SUMMARY
----
• A chemical symbol is a short universal code for an element's name so scientists everywhere understand each other.
• The first letter of a symbol is ALWAYS a capital letter. If there is a second letter, it MUST be a small letter.
• Example: calcium is Ca, not CA or ca. Copper is Cu. Cobalt is Co — but CO (both capitals) means the compound carbon monoxide, not cobalt.
• Some symbols come from English names (H, O, C). Others come from Latin names (Na from Natrium for sodium, Fe from Ferrum for iron).

REVISION QUESTIONS
----

3. A learner makes a mistake about rules for writing chemical symbols. State a likely wrong idea, correct it, and justify your correction with facts from this page.

ANSWERS
----
1. A chemical symbol is a short universal code for an element's name so scientists everywhere understand each other. For example, link it to a real object or event at home, school, market or shamba that fits this page.
2. At a school lab in Machakos, you would observe something that matches rules for writing chemical symbols. Name the observation, then explain it using the definition above. End by stating why the correct idea matters for accuracy or safety.
3. Wrong idea: confusing rules for writing chemical symbols with a neighbouring concept or ignoring a key rule. Correct idea: Capitalization and universal use of symbols. Justification: the worked example on this page shows the right reasoning with real objects or numbers.

studyPages.title: Symbols from English Names
studyPages.body:
SYMBOLS FROM ENGLISH NAMES
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what symbols from english names means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show symbols from english names.
• Correct one common mistake about symbols from english names.

INTRODUCTION
----
Many element symbols are simply shortened English names: H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, C for carbon, N for nitrogen. That shortcut saves time in formulas like H₂O, but only if you keep the letters exact — N is nitrogen, never helium.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Hydrogen has the symbol H.
• Helium has the symbol He.
• Carbon has the symbol C.
• Nitrogen has the symbol N.
• Oxygen has the symbol O.
• Fluorine has the symbol F.
• Neon has the symbol Ne.
• Magnesium has the symbol Mg.
• Aluminium has the symbol Al.
• Chlorine has the symbol Cl.
• Calcium has the symbol Ca.
• These symbols come from the English names of the elements.

Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. studyPages.title: Symbols from Latin Names
studyPages.body:
SYMBOLS FROM LATIN NAMES
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what symbols from latin names means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show symbols from latin names.
• Correct one common mistake about symbols from latin names.

INTRODUCTION
----
Why is iron Fe and sodium Na? Those letters come from older Latin names — Ferrum and Natrium — still used so the symbol stays the same worldwide. Learning a few Latin roots stops you guessing wrong letters in an exam.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Sodium has the symbol Na, from the Latin name Natrium.
• Potassium has the symbol K, from the Latin name Kalium.
• Iron has the symbol Fe, from the Latin name Ferrum.
• Copper has the symbol Cu, from the Latin name Cuprum.
• Silver has the symbol Ag, from the Latin name Argentum.
• Gold has the symbol Au, from the Latin name Aurum.
• Lead has the symbol Pb, from the Latin name Plumbum.
• Mercury has the symbol Hg, from the Latin name Hydrargyrum.
• Learning the Latin root helps you remember symbols that do not match the English spelling.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked situation (a boarding school dining hall in Eldoret): a learner investigates symbols from latin names. First observation: Copper represented by Cu from Latin word cuprum. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a boarding school dining hall in Eldoret, symbols from latin names shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Safety tip: protect your eyes when heating and never taste unknown chemicals.

SUMMARY
----
• Sodium has the symbol Na, from the Latin name Natrium.
• Potassium has the symbol K, from the Latin name Kalium.
• Iron has the symbol Fe, from the Latin name Ferrum.
• Copper has the symbol Cu, from the Latin name Cuprum.

ANSWERS

2. At a boarding school dining hall in Eldoret, you would observe something that matches symbols from latin names. Name the observation, then explain it using the definition above. End by stating why the correct idea matters for accuracy or safety.
